title: The blind leading the blind
hookLine: a line of people, hands on shoulders, sure of the way. none of them can see
carry: a true teacher: learned, and rooted in brahman
tomorrow: is a hard question for a teacher doubt, or respect?
last: HONOR THE LAMP. LOOK AT THE LIGHT.

lines: HANDS ON SHOULDERS, SURE OF THE WAY.
cards: On a trail you've never walked, it's easy to just follow the person in front and trust they know the way. An old Upanishad draws a line like that.
People walk down a road, each with a hand on the shoulder of the one ahead. They move with confidence. They're sure of the way.
Not one of them can see, and that includes the one at the front.

teach.b: The Mundaka Upanishad opens with a story. Shaunaka, a great householder, comes to the sage Angiras in the proper way and asks one question: what is that, by knowing which, everything is known?
Angiras answers that there are two kinds of knowledge, a lower and a higher. And then he paints the warning.

teach.h: THE BLIND LED BY THE BLIND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: people living in ignorance, wise in their own eyes, puffed up with learning, wander round and round, like the blind led by the blind. The remedy follows.

A seeker who wants to know the truth should go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is two things: shrotriya, learned in the Veda, and brahmanishtha, established in Brahman, settled in the reality the texts point to.

The fuel was the student's humble gift, sticks for the teacher's sacred fire. The two marks belong together. Learning alone can be the one at the front of the line, quoting beautifully and seeing nothing.
Notice what's missing: a following, a well-known name, a striking personality. Now hold up the week.
Narada, a servant boy who learned by hearing the sages sing.

teach.h: A WEEK OF THE NAMES, AND A TEST.
teach.b: Arjuna's chariot, and a mind kept on Krishna. Haridasa's hut. Grass, and a tree that gives shade.

teach.h: LEARNED, AND ROOTED, BOTH AT ONCE.
teach.b: Vidura's plain meal. Ekalavya's thumb. And a line of the blind, with a test that's quiet and hard to fake.

how: Hindus looking for a teacher weigh learning and character; the Mundaka Upanishad's two marks, shrotriya and brahmanishtha, give words for both.

games.q: what does “modern gurus and their cautions” mean?
o: teachers honored deeply, and the texts' tests for telling true ones
a warning never to trust any spiritual teacher at all
well-known Indian teachers who became celebrities in the West

games.q: the oldest caution — tap the pairs.
p: the blind led by the blind

s: the Upanishad's ideal teacher is marked by a large following
its two marks are learning in the Veda and being established in Brahman.
the Mundaka Upanishad warns of the blind leading the blind
people wise in their own eyes wander round and round, like the blind led by the blind.
the seeker in the verse arrives empty-handed
the seeker comes fuel in hand, a humble gift for the teacher's fire.

games.q: a friend quotes scripture perfectly, every time, but he's cruel to his little sister. by the Mundaka's two marks, what's missing?
o: rooted: he's learned, but not living what the texts point to.
nothing: knowing the texts that well is the whole test.
learning: he needs to memorize even more of the texts.
games.why: shrotriya and brahmanishtha: learned, and established in what the texts point to. learning alone can be the one at the front of the line, quoting beautifully and seeing nothing.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly across the room and back, eyes open, noticing each thing you'd miss if you were only following someone's shoulder.
If walking isn't possible right now, rest your open hands in your lap as if carrying a small bundle of sticks, the student's gift, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Modern gurus and their cautions: today, two marks of a real teacher, and a road full of the blind.

orig.note: Sanskrit: brahmanishtha, established in Brahman, the Mundaka's second mark of a teacher.

carryVoice: Last line of the week, from the Mundaka: a true teacher is learned, and rooted in Brahman, both at once. That's the week.

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 1.1.3–4 (Shaunaka approaches Angiras and asks what, when known, makes all this known; Angiras speaks of two kinds of knowledge, lower and higher)
Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.8 (the ignorant, wise in their own eyes, go round and round like the blind led by the blind)
Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.12 (the seeker goes, fuel in hand, to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman)
